title: Shaking the palace
hookLine: Moggallana shakes the god Sakka's palace with his toe to wake him from pride

lines: SAKKA, KING OF THE GODS, ASKS.
A SHORT ANSWER. A HAPPY GOD.
cards: Sakka is king of the gods of the Thirty-Three, one of the heavens in Buddhist cosmology. One day he visits the Buddha and asks a big question in a few words: how is a monk freed by the ending of craving?
The Buddha answers briefly. Sakka is delighted, bows, and goes home to heaven. Then the monk Moggallana, sitting nearby, starts to wonder.
Did Sakka actually understand that, or did he just enjoy it?

teach.b: This is the shorter discourse on the ending of craving, the thirty-seventh of the Middle-Length Sayings. The heart of the Buddha's answer is one short phrase: nothing is worth clinging to.
A monk who has heard that knows everything directly, and whatever feeling comes, pleasant, painful or neither, he sees it as impermanent and lets it go.
So Moggallana travels to the heaven of the Thirty-Three to check.
He finds Sakka in a garden, surrounded by heavenly music. Asked about the teaching, Sakka brushes it aside: we gods are so busy. Instead, he shows off.

teach.h: A BIG TOE, AND THE PALACE TREMBLES
teach.b: Come and see my palace, the Vejayanta, built after our victory over the titans. Look at the towers. Look at the rooms.
Even the goddesses, shy at the sight of a visiting monk, slip away into their rooms. Moggallana thinks: this god is living too carelessly. So he uses his powers.
With his big toe, the text says, he makes the whole palace shake and quake and tremble. Sakka and his court are amazed, and their pride goes quiet.
Then Moggallana asks again: what did the Buddha tell you, briefly, about the ending of craving? This time Sakka repeats it, word for word. He had heard it the first time.
He just couldn't hear it from inside the palace. A teaching can delight someone and slide right past while they go back to admiring their towers. Sometimes it takes a little shaking.

how: Teachers quote the phrase 'nothing is worth clinging to' from this discourse, and use the story of Moggallana and Sakka to show that even pleasant, heavenly lives can make people careless about practice.

o: a palace, like the one the god showed off
a festival of lamps held in heaven
a temple tower built to hold a relic

games.q: who did what in heaven — tap the pairs.
p: king of the gods of the Thirty-Three
shakes the palace with his toe

s: Sakka had forgotten the teaching entirely
once the palace shook, he repeated it back word for word; he'd heard it, but pride drowned it out.
Moggallana went to heaven to check whether Sakka understood
he wondered whether the god had truly grasped it or only enjoyed it.
the palace was shaken by an earthquake
the text says Moggallana made it shake with his big toe.

games.q: you're Moggallana. you've come to check on a god who heard the Buddha teach, and instead he's giving you a tour of his palace. what do you do?
o: admire the palace politely and leave.
shake the palace, so his pride goes quiet.
games.why: Moggallana shakes the palace with his toe. amazed and humbled, Sakka then repeats the Buddha's teaching back exactly.

practice: Think of one thing you're quietly proud of and lean on, a skill, a title, a reputation, being the reasonable one, and picture it as a palace with towers. Gently, like a toe tapping the floor, ask: is this worth clinging to?
Then let the picture go and rest with the breath, which needs no palace.

wordCard.voice: pasada. Moggallana's toe on a god's floor: a little shock that wakes pride enough to hear the teaching.

orig.note: Pali pasada: palace, mansion. Sakka's palace is the Vejayanta pasada.

carryVoice: Your line: shake the palace. Even a god's towers aren't worth clinging to. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 37, Culatanhasankhaya Sutta (the shorter discourse on the destruction of craving)
